catalog_quote: pp. 93-94: "VI. Tones 1. THE ROLE OF TONES IN GENERAL The circumstances in which my study of Birri was carried out were on the whole unfavourable, and particularly in connection with points such as this, entailing special care, patience and time. Tone certainly plays an important role in Birri, but I cannot make an estimate, however rough, of its weight in comparison with neigh-bouring Sudanic ... tone is not so decisive as, e.g. in the Ndogo group. But in connection with other points, e.g. the conjugation of verbs ... tonality is absolutely essential in Birri as in the Bongo-Kresh group. 2. WORD TONE Even within the narrow limits of my Birri Vocabulary one can detect several couples of words differing only in tone. E.g.: goat inyi to tie ódó to cut ágá hand inyi ... 3. TONE IN THE SENTENCE In the course of these notes I have endeavoured to mark, whenever I could, the variations ..." Orthography (c. p. 83): "acute accent over a vowel stands for the high tone the grave accent stands for low tone N.B. Double vowels stand for ..." Table of Contents (p. 81): "Part I: Phonetics I. Tones): "... low tone, mugu acquires middle tones in both syllables."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Santandrea describes Birri as a tone language (high/low marked with acute/grave; lexical 'word tone' and sentence tone discussed) and, as far as the snippet-accessible text and Google's in-volume index show, gives no rule for word stress; the only phonological use of the word 'stress' in the work concerns the Belanda-Bviri (Ndogo-group) autonym Virí, said to carry high tone and the word's sole 'accent or stress' on its second syllable, which is not a statement about Birri.
new_statements.exceptions: none; NB the Introduction sentence '..is pronounced Virí, with a high tone in the second syllable, on which alone lies the "accent" or "stress" of the word' refers to 'the latter' = the (Belanda-)Bviri name, not to Birri, and must not be catalogued as a Birri stress statement.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described at word level ('word tone') and sentence level ('tone in the sentence'); nothing on stress domain. Evidence is snippet-level only: full pages 93-95 were not seen, so a passing remark on stress inside the Tones section cannot be fully excluded (Google's in-volume search found no such hit for 'stress'; 'accent' could not be counted before the IP was blocked).
new_statements.identity_note: Santandrea 1966 describes the Mboto dialect of Birri as spoken by a handful of migrants at Deim Zubeir (South Sudan), per the Glottolog record and the Introduction; Glottolog treats this as Birri [birr1240/bvq] without dialect codes. Do not confuse with Belanda Viri/Bviri (Ndogo group, Ubangian; Glottolog bela1256) -- the one 'stress' sentence in Santandrea's Introduction is about the Bviri autonym Virí, not about Birri. The Glottolog ref 'Otto 1978, Zeitschrift für Slawistik' attached to birr1240 is a mis-linked record.
